problem.statement_clinical: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) — ICD-10 E28.2, SNOMED 69878008

subjective.vernacular: Are your periods irregular, infrequent (fewer than 8 per year), very heavy, or have they stopped altogether?
subjective.why_it_matters: Oligo/anovulation is one of the three Rotterdam criteria for PCOS and distinguishes PCOS from other androgen-excess disorders.

subjective.vernacular: Have you noticed unwanted or excessive hair growth on your face, chest, abdomen, or back?
subjective.why_it_matters: Self-reported hirsutism suggests clinical hyperandrogenism, supporting PCOS and prompting Ferriman-Gallwey scoring.

subjective.vernacular: Do you have persistent or severe acne, especially on your jaw, chin, or back?
subjective.why_it_matters: Adult-onset or treatment-resistant acne is a marker of androgen excess and supports a hyperandrogenic PCOS phenotype.

subjective.vernacular: Have you noticed thinning hair or hair loss, particularly at the top or front of your scalp?
subjective.why_it_matters: Scalp hair thinning in a male-pattern distribution is a sign of androgen excess consistent with PCOS.

subjective.vernacular: Have you been trying to get pregnant without success, or has a doctor told you that you may have trouble conceiving?
subjective.why_it_matters: Anovulatory infertility is a major clinical consequence of PCOS and guides treatment planning.

subjective.vernacular: Have you gained weight recently, and if so, does most of it sit around your belly?
subjective.why_it_matters: Central adiposity worsens insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism, and the record shows prior overweight diagnosis now resolved.
subjective.value: Weight 185 lbs (2026-06-14); prior overweight diagnosis noted as resolved 2026-07-03; height 220 cm (2021) yields BMI ~18.9 — data inconsistency noted, height may be erroneous.
subjective.missing: Confirmed current height for accurate BMI; clarification of weight history and whether overweight is truly resolved.

subjective.vernacular: Do you have dark, velvety patches of skin in your armpits, neck, or groin? Do you feel very tired after eating or crave sweets often?
subjective.why_it_matters: Acanthosis nigricans and carbohydrate cravings suggest insulin resistance, which co-exists in up to 70% of PCOS cases.

subjective.vernacular: Have you been feeling persistently sad, anxious beyond your baseline social anxiety, or having trouble with your mood?
subjective.why_it_matters: Depression and anxiety occur at higher rates in PCOS; the record confirms social anxiety disorder, which may compound PCOS-related distress and care avoidance.
subjective.value: Social anxiety disorder documented; patient reports it makes attending appointments very difficult.
subjective.missing: Screening for depression (PHQ-9) and generalized anxiety (GAD-7) specific to PCOS context.

subjective.vernacular: Do you snore loudly, stop breathing during sleep, or wake up feeling unrefreshed?
subjective.why_it_matters: Obstructive sleep apnea is significantly more common in PCOS due to androgen effects and metabolic comorbidity.

subjective.vernacular: Do you have pain in your lower abdomen or pelvis, especially around your period or during sex?
subjective.why_it_matters: Chronic pelvic pain raises the possibility of endometriosis as a comorbidity or alternative diagnosis alongside PCOS.

subjective.vernacular: What birth control have you used, if any? Have you ever been pregnant? Any pregnancy complications like gestational diabetes?
subjective.why_it_matters: Hormonal contraception can mask PCOS symptoms; gestational diabetes history elevates type 2 diabetes risk in PCOS.

subjective.term: Family history of PCOS, diabetes, or cardiovascular disease
subjective.vernacular: Does anyone in your family have PCOS, irregular periods, diabetes, or heart disease at a young age?
subjective.why_it_matters: PCOS clusters in families and shares heritable risk with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, influencing long-term monitoring intensity.

objective.value: 2026-07-03 fhir-vital: 195/194 mmHg — critically elevated and likely erroneous or represents hypertensive emergency; 2026-06-13 SCP: 120/60 mmHg.
objective.missing: Repeat measurement to confirm or refute the 195/194 reading; if confirmed, hypertensive emergency workup supersedes PCOS frame.

objective.term: Body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference
objective.value: Weight 185 lbs (2026-06-14); height 220 cm (2021-01-11) — BMI implausibly low at ~18.9, height likely erroneous.
objective.missing: Accurate current height; waist circumference for central adiposity assessment.

objective.vernacular: Standardized scoring of body hair in 9 areas to measure androgen-related hair growth
Examination of the neck, armpits, and groin for dark, velvety skin patches
Blood tests measuring pituitary hormones that control the ovaries
Blood test reflecting the number of small follicles in the ovaries

objective.term: Fasting glucose and fasting insulin / HOMA-IR
objective.vernacular: Blood tests for blood sugar and insulin resistance
objective.value: HbA1c 5.1% (2019-05-28) — normal range, no diabetes at that time.
objective.missing: Current fasting glucose, fasting insulin, and repeat HbA1c — 7-year interval is too long for ongoing PCOS metabolic monitoring.

objective.vernacular: Blood test for cholesterol and triglycerides
Blood test for a pituitary hormone that can disrupt periods if elevated
Ultrasound of the ovaries and uterus to count follicles and assess ovarian volume
Blood test to rule out a congenital adrenal enzyme deficiency that mimics PCOS
Blood test measuring an adrenal androgen to distinguish adrenal from ovarian androgen excess

assessment_candidates.term: PCOS — classic hyperandrogenic anovulatory phenotype (Rotterdam phenotype A)
assessment_candidates.vernacular: The most common form of PCOS: irregular periods, elevated male hormones, and polycystic-appearing ovaries on ultrasound
assessment_candidates.basis: Diagnosis on record since 2005; Rotterdam 2003 criteria require 2 of 3 features: oligo/anovulation, clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovarian morphology. Phenotype A is most prevalent (~50% of PCOS).
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Diagnosis is established by record, but current phenotype, severity, and metabolic status are unknown without recent testing.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated PCOS carries long-term risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, endometrial cancer, and infertility — these harms accumulate silently over years.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: PCOS combined with abdominal obesity, high blood pressure, abnormal blood fats, and high blood sugar
not_yet_testable: o-008 (current fasting glucose/insulin — not yet ordered)
assessment_candidates.basis: Metabolic syndrome occurs in 30–40% of PCOS patients; prior overweight diagnosis and potentially elevated BP (pending confirmation) raise concern; HbA1c was normal in 2019 but 7 years have elapsed.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot confirm or exclude without current fasting glucose, lipid panel, and accurate anthropometrics; the 195/194 BP reading requires urgent repeat.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Metabolic syndrome with PCOS markedly raises lifetime risk of heart attack, stroke, and type 2 diabetes — serious irreversible harm if unaddressed.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A genetic enzyme deficiency that causes the adrenal glands to overproduce male hormones, closely mimicking PCOS
assessment_candidates.basis: NC-CAH affects ~1–2% of women presenting with PCOS features; guidelines recommend 17-OHP screening in hyperandrogenic women, especially those of relevant ancestry.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot assess without 17-OHP; cannot exclude on clinical grounds alone given absent biochemical workup.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Missed NC-CAH means treating the wrong condition — symptoms persist and glucocorticoid treatment that would work is never given.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: An underactive thyroid that can cause irregular periods and weight gain, overlapping with or worsening PCOS
assessment_candidates.basis: Hypothyroidism is a common and easily reversible cause of menstrual irregularity; guidelines recommend TSH in all women with suspected PCOS to exclude thyroid disease.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot assess without TSH; may coexist with PCOS rather than replace it as a diagnosis.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated hypothyroidism worsens PCOS symptoms and metabolic risk but is highly correctable with thyroid replacement therapy.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Elevated prolactin from a pituitary gland abnormality causing irregular periods that can look like PCOS
assessment_candidates.basis: Hyperprolactinemia causes anovulation and menstrual irregularity; it is a required exclusion before confirming PCOS per guidelines.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: No prolactin result available; low prior probability but must be formally excluded.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Undiagnosed pituitary adenoma causing hyperprolactinemia can enlarge and compress surrounding structures if not treated.

assessment_candidates.term: PCOS-associated endometrial hyperplasia or endometrial cancer risk
assessment_candidates.vernacular: Thickening of the uterine lining due to prolonged lack of ovulation, raising cancer risk
not_yet_testable: o-012 (pelvic ultrasound with endometrial thickness — not yet ordered)
assessment_candidates.basis: Chronic anovulation exposes the endometrium to unopposed estrogen; women with PCOS have a 3-fold increased risk of endometrial cancer; relevant given age 38 and possible long-standing anovulation.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Risk is determined by duration and degree of anovulation — both unknown without menstrual history and ultrasound.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Endometrial cancer is life-threatening if not detected early; long-term unmonitored anovulation is the key risk driver.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A rare tumor producing male hormones, which can mimic or coexist with PCOS
not_yet_testable: o-005 (testosterone — markedly elevated would prompt imaging)
o-014 (DHEAS — markedly elevated would suggest adrenal source)
assessment_candidates.basis: Rare but important — testosterone >150–200 ng/dL or rapidly progressive virilization suggests tumor rather than PCOS; included because biochemical data are absent.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Very low probability in the absence of rapid virilization history, but cannot be excluded without testosterone measurement.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: An undetected androgen-secreting tumor can be malignant and is life-threatening if not found and removed.

residual.vernacular: Something not on this list — the differential is never closed

plan_options.vernacular: Blood tests for total testosterone, free testosterone, DHEAS, and sex-hormone binding globulin
plan_options.basis: Endocrine Society PCOS Guideline 2023 recommends biochemical androgen measurement to confirm hyperandrogenism; free testosterone is the most sensitive marker.

plan_options.vernacular: Ovarian ultrasound to count follicles (≥20 per ovary) and measure ovarian volume (≥10 mL) per Rotterdam criteria
plan_options.basis: Rotterdam 2003 criteria; threshold updated to ≥20 follicles per ovary with modern high-frequency probes (Teede et al. 2023 international guideline).
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician; performed by radiology or gynecology

plan_options.vernacular: Fasting glucose, fasting insulin, HbA1c, and full lipid panel to check for diabetes risk and abnormal cholesterol
plan_options.basis: AES and Endocrine Society guidelines recommend metabolic screening at diagnosis and every 1–2 years in PCOS; last HbA1c was 2019.

plan_options.vernacular: TSH, prolactin, LH, FSH, and early-morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone to rule out thyroid disease, pituitary tumor, and congenital adrenal hyperplasia
plan_options.basis: Rotterdam consensus and Endocrine Society PCOS guideline mandate exclusion of these mimics before confirming PCOS.

plan_options.vernacular: Confirm or refute the 195/194 mmHg reading with an immediate repeat measurement; if confirmed, treat as hypertensive emergency
plan_options.basis: BP 195/194 mmHg, if accurate, meets criteria for hypertensive emergency (AHA/ACC); this is a patient-safety priority independent of PCOS.
plan_options.who_can_act: Any clinician or trained healthcare worker; emergency services if confirmed at home

plan_options.term: Combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) for cycle regulation and androgen suppression
plan_options.vernacular: Birth control pill used to regulate periods, reduce acne and excess hair, and protect the uterine lining
plan_options.basis: First-line pharmacotherapy for non-fertility PCOS symptoms per Endocrine Society and ESHRE/ASRM guidelines; also reduces endometrial hyperplasia risk.

plan_options.term: Metformin for insulin resistance and metabolic risk
plan_options.vernacular: Oral diabetes medication used in PCOS to improve insulin sensitivity, assist with weight, and reduce diabetes risk
plan_options.basis: Recommended as adjunct to lifestyle in PCOS with metabolic risk or when COCP is not tolerated (Teede et al. 2023 international PCOS guideline).

plan_options.term: Lifestyle intervention — low-GI dietary pattern and progressive physical activity
plan_options.vernacular: Structured eating plan focusing on low-sugar foods, combined with gradual increase in exercise, to improve hormones and metabolic health
plan_options.basis: Even 5–10% weight reduction in overweight PCOS patients restores ovulation and reduces metabolic risk (Teede et al. 2023); active nutrition goals already in care plan support this.
plan_options.who_can_act: Registered dietitian, exercise physiologist, primary care team; patient self-directed with guidance

plan_options.vernacular: Ensuring regular progestogen exposure (via COCP, progestogen-only pill, or IUD) to prevent uterine lining build-up
plan_options.basis: Women with PCOS who are anovulatory require at least 4 withdrawal bleeds per year to protect against endometrial hyperplasia (RCOG/Endocrine Society).

plan_options.vernacular: Arranging telehealth, home blood draws, or visits with a trusted support person to reduce barriers caused by social anxiety
plan_options.basis: Patient explicitly identifies social anxiety and mobility/transportation challenges as barriers; care should be adapted to these needs to prevent disengagement (PCOS guideline section on psychosocial care, Teede 2023).
plan_options.who_can_act: Care coordinator, primary care team, behavioral health provider
